I'm reading the "Everything you need to know about...." link. I like it!

Do check out /v/SSL and feel free to contribute!

Are you looking for symmetric or asymmetric algorithms? I.e. what are you trying to do?

For symmetric algorithms, I really like TwoFish .

If you're looking for asymmetric algorithms, it really comes down to what it is you're trying to do. If you're looking for a general purpose suite (which, you'll find your asymmetric algorithms are all suites of algorithms) you can't really go wrong with some variety of SSL. That said, I suspect there will be considerable debate as to which flavor of SSL one should use. That's mostly a function of the shit-debacle which was the heartbleed and similar fiascoes that SSL experienced in 2014.

If you're looking for something more purposed, you should probably give us the details of what you are trying to do, then we can advise accordingly.

For encryption in place, I saw they suggested GPG in one place. One of the other links suggested AES-256. I would probably go with the latter, but only because I am familiar with AES and not with GPG. AES-256 using cipher block chaining (CBC) and PKCS7 padding. NSA approves that configuration for storing TS information, so it should be OK for credit card data, etc.

Speaking of money, I think a lot of banks use TDES. The slide show recommends against it, but TDES's main "problem" that I know of is that it is slow. It is still very resistant to cryptanalysis.

The last symmetrical cipher I'll mention is Serpent. It was one of the 5 AES finalists, and the literature seems to have it one of the most secure. It was slower than Rijndael (the winner) though -- still faster than TDES, I think -- so this is why it did not win. So Serpent is fascinating to me. But that is just a rock-solid toy. If I am storing other people's data that is worth money, I'll use AES-256 so if it breaks I don't have to explain to everyone why I was using a non-standard algorithm.

For secure communications over insecure networks, of course you would use an asymmetrical algorithm to pass a session key to a symmetrical algorithm, then communicate for the rest of the session using that symmetrical algorithm. This is because symmetrical algorithms can encrypt and decrypt many times faster than asymmetrical ones can. Also I think they are more resistant to compromise from key reuse (just use a key for the one session and then discard it, though). For the asymmetrical algorithm, Elliptic Curve seems to be well trusted these days. I have heard of a lattice-based crypto one flavor of which is NTRU which sounds promising. But NTRU is still not vetted enough. I'd use Elliptic Curve if I had to choose a specific algorithm.
